comments.body:
> **Marcus** · cohort peer

Contrarian view: is this not over-cautious? The cost model in notebook 07 uses published per-token prices and real token counts. The arithmetic is arithmetic. If a client asks "roughly what does a query cost", saying "about a cent" is more useful than refusing to answer.

I understand not quoting the *recall* numbers. But cost seems different in kind.

replies.body:
> **Dana** · reviewer · owns the eval harness

The distinction you are drawing is real and I want to agree with half of it, then show you where the half that is wrong actually bites.

**You are right that cost and quality are different in kind.** Quality numbers are corpus-dependent in a way that makes them nearly meaningless off this corpus. Token counts are more portable — a 4,000-token prompt is 4,000 tokens anywhere.

**Where it breaks is that the per-query price is not the number a client is asking for.** They are asking what the *system* costs, and the query price is typically a minority of it. Off notebook 07's own model, for a mid-size deployment:

```
                              share of monthly bill
generation tokens                      31%
embedding — initial backfill           18%   (one-off, but it lands in month one)
embedding — re-embed on drift          14%   (recurring, always forgotten)
vector store / OpenSearch cluster      22%   (fixed, does not scale down)
reranker inference                      9%
trace + eval storage                    6%
```

Quote "about a cent a query" and you have described **31%** of the bill with high confidence and implied the other 69% is rounding. That is the conversation that goes badly in month three, and it goes badly *because* the number you gave was accurate.

**What is safe to say**, and it is genuinely useful:

> "The per-query token cost is around X, and I can show you the model. It is roughly a third of the total — the cluster and the re-embedding cycle dominate, and both depend on facts about your corpus I do not have yet. Give me your document count and change rate and I will turn this into a real number in a week."

That is more credible than a confident cent-per-query, not less. **The methodology transfers; the constants do not** — and saying which is which is the thing that makes a client trust the next number you give them.

> **Marcus** · cohort peer

The 31% breakdown is the argument. I was going to quote a number that was true and load-bearing for the wrong conclusion.
